title: DepthWizard - Single-View Height Estimation and 3D Flythrough

description:
Background Accurate Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and Digital Surface Models (DSMs) are fundamental to urban planning, disaster management, and military reconnaissance. Traditionally, elevation data is acquired through stereo-imaging pairs, LiDAR, or Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR). These approaches can be cost-prohibitive, dependent on specific sensor availability, and computationally intensive. Single-view height estimation offers an agile alternative, but foundational monocular depth models are trained largely on natural egocentric imagery and predict relative depth. When applied to remote sensing, they face domain gaps, structural variations, and a lack of absolute-scale mapping. Converting relative depth into metric elevation remains a critical challenge, alongside the operational need to transform static elevation profiles into interactive 3D assets that can be navigated in real time.
Description Develop an end-to-end software pipeline that transforms single-view optical RGB remote-sensing images into high-precision elevation maps. The framework must support both non-georeferenced and georeferenced imagery.
• Non-Georeferenced RGB Imagery (for example, PNG or JPG): Produce a Relative Digital Surface Model (rDSM) for images without spatial metadata.
• Georeferenced RGB Imagery (for example, GeoTIFF): Produce an Absolute Digital Surface Model (DSM) with metric height values for images containing coordinate-system metadata.
The solution should use a pre-trained monocular depth-estimation backbone to generate initial relative-depth maps. For georeferenced imagery, a lower-resolution DEM source such as SRTM or a limited set of Ground Control Points may be used to map scale-agnostic depth features to absolute metric elevations. For non-georeferenced imagery, relative height may be used directly in the visualization stage.
After computing the elevation map, the system should project the original optical image onto a generated 3D terrain mesh and integrate the result with a rendering engine such as Unity, Three.js, or Babylon.js. The interface should support seamless first-person navigation and analysis of structural heights and slopes from arbitrary aerial perspectives.
Key Milestones
• Elevation Extraction: Use a robust pre-trained monocular depth model to extract geometric and structural representations from single-view optical imagery.
• Scale Calibration: Develop a module that converts relative depth to absolute height using scene-level statistics, low-resolution DEMs, semantic priors, or minimal Ground Control Points for georeferenced inputs.
• Visualization Layer: Build an immersive, preferably interactive, rendering pipeline that converts the optical texture and derived depth map into a navigable 3D environment deployable as a standalone application.
Evaluation Criteria:
• DSM Estimation - Accuracy and Validation (50%): Evaluate RMSE, MAE, and correlation against LiDAR or reference data, including performance stability across urban, sparse, hilly, and forested landscapes.
• Visualization - Rendering Quality and User Experience (50%): Assess projection accuracy, visual fidelity, navigability of the 3D flythrough, interface intuitiveness, software stability, and successful standalone deployment.
Expected Solution Deliver a fully integrated software suite with complete source code and technical documentation. The solution must be deployable as a unified module containing the following components:
• Elevation Estimation Module: Accept single-view optical satellite imagery in PNG, JPG, or TIFF format and output a high-fidelity DSM in a standard geospatial format.
• Interactive Visualization Platform: Provide a user-friendly 3D flythrough experience that lets users upload imagery, visualize reconstructed terrain, and validate estimated height values against reference datasets.
summary: Innovation (3/5): draws on satellite applied to a miscellaneous problem, placing it in the moderate band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (3/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Miscellaneous. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on sensor, model, standard. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (2/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 19/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: DepthWizard - Single-View Height Estimation and 3D Flythrough

overview.in_plain_terms: Take a single flat satellite or aerial photo and turn it into an elevation map, then a navigable 3D scene, without needing the expensive stereo-imaging, LiDAR, or radar equipment traditionally required to measure height from above.
overview.why_it_matters: Accurate elevation data feeds urban planning, disaster management, and reconnaissance, but the usual ways to get it are expensive and sensor-dependent. If a single ordinary image can produce a usable elevation map, that unlocks elevation data anywhere a camera already exists.
pain_points: Traditional elevation data (stereo pairs, LiDAR, InSAR) is cost-prohibitive and sensor-dependent.
Off-the-shelf monocular depth models predict only relative depth, not real-world metric height, and they're trained on ground-level photos, not remote-sensing imagery.
Static elevation data isn't very useful on its own, it needs to become an interactive, navigable 3D scene to actually be usable.
overview.background: Digital Elevation/Surface Models are fundamental to urban planning, disaster management, and reconnaissance, but traditional acquisition methods are expensive and computationally intensive. Foundational monocular depth models exist but are trained on natural, ground-level imagery and only predict relative depth, converting that into absolute metric elevation for remote-sensing images remains an unsolved gap.
overview.whats_being_asked: An end-to-end pipeline that converts single-view optical RGB remote-sensing images into high-precision elevation maps, supporting both non-georeferenced imagery (producing a relative surface model) and georeferenced imagery (producing an absolute metric surface model), then projecting the result into a navigable 3D terrain mesh.
expected_solution: For non-georeferenced RGB imagery: produce a Relative Digital Surface Model (rDSM).
For georeferenced imagery (e.g. GeoTIFF): produce an Absolute DSM with metric height values, using a reference DEM (like SRTM) or ground control points to convert relative to absolute scale.
Use a pretrained monocular depth-estimation backbone as the starting point for the relative-depth prediction.
Project the original image onto the generated 3D terrain mesh for a navigable 3D flythrough view.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Moderate band, and that's the accurate read, monocular depth estimation is a well-established research area, the innovation here is the domain adaptation (natural-image models to remote-sensing) and the relative-to-absolute scale conversion, which is a real, non-trivial engineering problem, not a novel algorithm.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. You need a depth-estimation pipeline, a scale-recovery mechanism for georeferenced inputs, and a 3D mesh-generation/visualization layer, three genuinely distinct technical components chained together.

competitive_landscape.note: Remote-sensing-specific computer vision PS types are rarer at SIH than generic app-building PS, this will draw a smaller, more geospatial/CV-comfortable field.

innovation.note: Applies known monocular-depth techniques to a domain (remote sensing) where they aren't natively trained, the adaptation is the real contribution, not a new algorithm.

invention.note: Depth prediction, scale recovery from reference DEM/GCPs, and 3D mesh generation are three separate, non-trivial subsystems.

technical_feasibility.note: Getting real georeferenced GeoTIFF test imagery plus a reference DEM to validate absolute scale is the hardest part, plan your data sourcing before you plan your model.

impact_and_benefits.note: This is an infrastructure/tooling PS rather than a direct citizen-facing one, its impact case rests on downstream uses (planning, disaster response) rather than an obvious immediate user.

architecture.note: Depth model -> scale correction -> mesh generation -> texture projection -> interactive viewer is a genuinely long pipeline where any one broken link kills the demo.

overall_verdict.reasoning: A good pick for a team with computer vision and some 3D graphics comfort, but be realistic: doing both the non-georeferenced and georeferenced paths well in 36 hours is a stretch. Nail the relative-depth + 3D-flythrough path first since it's demo-friendly on its own, then add absolute scale conversion as a stretch goal if time allows.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: The 3D flythrough output is inherently visual and impressive on stage, a static elevation map is forgettable, a navigable 3D scene generated from one photo is not.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Chasing full absolute-metric accuracy against a real reference DEM is a rabbit hole, teams can burn most of their time on scale calibration and end up with no working 3D visualization at all, that's the wrong tradeoff for a hackathon demo.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm hour 0: do you have access to sample georeferenced GeoTIFF imagery and a reference elevation source (SRTM is free and downloadable)? If sourcing that data will eat hours, prioritize the non-georeferenced relative-depth path for your primary demo.

idea_0_4: Decide primary demo path: relative depth + 3D flythrough on non-georeferenced imagery (safer, faster) with absolute-scale conversion as a stretch goal, not the core deliverable.
Source test imagery immediately, satellite/aerial photos of varied terrain (urban, hilly), plus one sample GeoTIFF with known elevation ground truth if pursuing the stretch goal.
Split ownership: one person on the depth-estimation pipeline, one on 3D mesh generation/texturing, one on data sourcing and the scale-conversion math.
prototype_4_22: Get a pretrained monocular depth model (e.g. MiDaS, Depth Anything) running on your remote-sensing test images, expect quality issues since it's out-of-domain, that's expected and worth noting honestly.
Build the relative-depth-to-3D-mesh pipeline: generate a terrain mesh from the depth map and project the original texture onto it.
In parallel, prototype the absolute-scale recovery using SRTM data or ground control points on your GeoTIFF sample.
integration_22_30: Wire the full non-georeferenced path end to end: image in -> depth map -> mesh -> textured 3D scene you can navigate.
If the georeferenced/absolute-scale path is working, integrate it as a second mode; if it's not solid, cut it rather than risk it breaking live.
Build a simple interactive viewer (web-based 3D viewer works well) for the flythrough.
polish_30_36: Rehearse navigating the 3D flythrough live, this is your headline demo moment, make sure it's smooth and doesn't lag.
Prepare a clear before/after visual: flat photo on one side, navigable 3D scene on the other.
Be ready to honestly explain domain-gap limitations (out-of-domain depth model accuracy) rather than overclaiming precision.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Let judges themselves navigate the 3D flythrough live, on their own device or yours, handing over control is more convincing than you narrating a fixed camera path.

strengths: The 3D flythrough output is a strong, visual, hard-to-fake demo centerpiece.
Pretrained depth-estimation backbones give you a real head start instead of training from scratch.
weaknesses: Domain gap between natural-image training data and remote-sensing input means raw model accuracy will be rough without fine-tuning.
Absolute-scale conversion (the georeferenced path) is a legitimately hard sub-problem that can consume disproportionate time for uncertain payoff.

roles_needed: 3D graphics developer (mesh generation, texture projection, viewer)
Someone comfortable with geospatial data (GeoTIFF, DEMs) for the stretch goal
team_fit.ideal_ratio: 1 CV, 1 graphics, 1 geospatial/data-focused, each subsystem genuinely needs its own owner.
team_fit.approach: Get the CV and graphics halves working independently against a shared sample image early, then integrate, don't build them serially or the graphics person sits idle waiting on depth output.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Pretrained depth-model integration, mesh-generation boilerplate, and a basic 3D web viewer can all be scaffolded quickly with AI coding assistance.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Assessing whether the depth output is remotely plausible for remote-sensing imagery (versus obviously broken due to domain gap) needs a human eyeballing the output, this isn't something to blindly trust from the model.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-suggested pipeline that treats the pretrained depth model's output as ground truth without domain-gap validation will produce a visually broken or nonsensical 3D mesh, spend real time sanity-checking outputs against known terrain.

data_resource_availability.status: Free satellite/aerial imagery is broadly available (Google Earth exports, open aerial datasets); SRTM elevation data is free and downloadable for the absolute-scale stretch goal.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If real georeferenced test data is hard to source in time, demo the relative-depth + 3D flythrough path exclusively and describe the absolute-scale extension conceptually rather than half-building it.

judge_qna.question: How accurate is your elevation estimate compared to ground truth?
judge_qna.strong_answer: For the relative-depth path we're honest that it's qualitative, not metric; for the absolute-scale path, we validated against SRTM reference data on our sample image and can show the measured error.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's driving the largest source of error, the depth model itself or the scale-conversion step?

judge_qna.question: Why not just use existing stereo-imaging or LiDAR pipelines instead of single-view estimation?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Those need specific sensor hardware and are expensive to deploy broadly, our approach works from any single existing photo, which massively widens where elevation data can be generated from.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's the tradeoff in accuracy you're accepting to get that broader applicability?

judge_qna.question: What happens with imagery from a domain your depth model wasn't trained on, e.g. dense forest canopy?
judge_qna.strong_answer: We'd expect degraded accuracy since it's further from the model's training distribution, that's a known limitation we'd flag rather than hide, and it's a natural next step for fine-tuning on remote-sensing-specific data.
judge_qna.follow_up: How would you go about collecting fine-tuning data for that domain gap?
